sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: The chapter gives a conceptual cost estimate method that identifies the components with the largest effect on cost before bid quantities and bidders are known. It starts from a baseline price: in 2004 a reasonable average was about $300 per linear meter of micropile, considered appropriate for any US region and project type, after a decade of falling costs from contractor experience and better equipment. The baseline is adjusted for project-specific constraints.
sections.body: (p. 10-1) The chapter presents an approach for a cost estimate for any micropile project, similar to a conceptual cost estimate in engineering: enough detail to identify the cost components with the largest effect on total cost, although specific bid quantities and potential bidders are not necessarily known. The method requires a known baseline cost. Over the past ten years numerous micropile projects have been completed in the United States and typical costs have decreased, mostly from experience gained by specialty contractors and advances in installation equipment. In 2004 a reasonable 'average' price for micropiles is on the order of $300 per linear meter of micropile, considered appropriate for any region of the U.S. and any type of micropile project. The method adjusts this baseline for project-specific technical and non-technical constraints; the key factors affecting cost are discussed first.
key_points: Conceptual cost estimate: identifies the components with the largest effect on cost before bid quantities are known
Baseline 2004 average price about $300 per linear meter of micropile, for any US region and project type
Costs fell over the prior decade with contractor experience and equipment advances
The baseline is adjusted for project-specific technical and non-technical constraints (Table 10-4)
sections.applicability: The conceptual cost estimating approach for micropiles and its 2004 baseline price.

sections.summary: Table 10-1 gives typical ranges of micropile unit cost: material 25 to 40 percent, equipment 20 to 30 percent, labor 25 to 60 percent and load testing less than 5 percent. Load testing is listed separately and is often a separate pay item.

sections.title: Micropile Material Costs
sections.summary: Principal materials are threaded casing, grout, reinforcing bars and centralizers; structural steel is significant. Common US casings are 140, 175 and 241 mm (Table 10-2 lists 139.7, 177.8 and 244.5 mm) at $15-25, $35-45 and $50-60 per meter unthreaded (early 2004). Threading both ends costs $50 to $70 per casing: about $60 for a 1-m 140-mm section costing $20, so short sections are costly. Bars of 57 and 64 mm cost $20-26 and $26-32 per meter (Table 10-3).
sections.body: (pp. 10-1 to 10-3) The principal material components are threaded steel casings, cement grout, steel reinforcing bars and centralizers; with the higher load capacities micropiles continue to achieve, structural steel is a significant cost component. Threaded Steel Casing: the most common US casings have outside diameters of 140 mm (5.5 in.), 175 mm (7 in.) and 241 mm (9-5/8 in.) (as printed in the text; Table 10-2 lists 139.7, 177.8 and 244.5 mm); costs without threads are in Table 10-2, subject to relatively large fluctuations in steel prices and representative of 2004, and previously used casings may reduce material cost. Low headroom or difficult access often requires short casing sections joined by flush threaded joints; threading both ends (male and female) typically costs $50 to $70 (2004) per casing, so where short lengths are required threading can be significant and the Owner should assess the required section lengths. For example, a 1-m 140-mm casing may cost about $20 while threading each 1-m section costs about $60, or 3 times the casing cost; the threading of a 4-m 140-mm casing would cost less than the casing itself. Steel Reinforcing Rods: the most common bars have outside diameters of 57 mm (2-1/4 in.) and 64 mm (2-1/2 in.), with 2004 costs in Table 10-3; centralizer material costs are relatively insignificant.
key_points: Principal materials: threaded steel casing, cement grout, reinforcing bars, centralizers; structural steel is a significant cost
Table 10-2 (early 2004, unthreaded): 139.7 mm x 10.5 mm wall $15-25/m; 177.8 mm x 12.6 mm $35-45/m; 244.5 mm x 13.8 mm $50-60/m
Threading both ends costs $50 to $70 per casing (2004): about $60 for a 1-m 140-mm section costing $20
Short casing sections (low headroom, difficult access) make threading costs significant; assess section lengths
Centralizer material costs are relatively insignificant

sections.title: Equipment Cost
sections.summary: Equipment costs have fallen with greater availability of drilling and grouting equipment. They are fixed costs for a contractor but linked to ground conditions and ease of drilling: drilling in very hard or bouldery ground to great depth (say more than 30 m) is significant. Smaller equipment may cost less, but very tight access with low headroom (say less than 3 m) and difficult drilling needs specialized equipment, which may be a significant cost.
sections.body: (p. 10-3) Overall equipment costs for micropile projects have decreased in recent years, mostly from greater availability of drilling and grouting equipment. Specific equipment costs are difficult to assign, since they are fixed costs for a contractor on a given project, but the Owner should recognize that drilling equipment costs are linked to ground conditions and the ease of drilling: drilling in excessively hard or bouldery ground to relatively great depths (e.g., greater than say 30 m (100 ft)) will be significant. Smaller drilling equipment is usually less costly than larger equipment, but very tight access with low headroom (e.g., less than say 3 m (10 ft)) and difficult drilling require specialized equipment, which, depending on the specialty contractor, may be a significant cost.
key_points: Equipment costs have fallen with greater availability of drilling and grouting equipment
Drilling cost is linked to ground conditions: hard or bouldery ground to more than about 30 m (100 ft) is significant
Very tight access with headroom below about 3 m (10 ft) and difficult drilling needs specialized, possibly costly equipment
sections.applicability: How ground, depth and access affect micropile equipment costs.

sections.title: Labor Cost
sections.summary: A typical crew is four: a superintendent, a drill operator and two laborers. With easy drilling and low to moderate capacities a crew may install 6 to 20 micropiles up to 15 m long per day, and labor is 25 to 30 percent of total cost; tight access and difficult drilling raise it to 30 to 45 percent, and labor-intensive work where labor costs are high (major urban areas) up to 60 percent.
sections.body: (p. 10-4) A typical micropile crew consists of four individuals: a project superintendent, a drilling operator and two laborers. The effect of labor on unit costs is directly linked to the ease of installation and daily installation rates. For relatively easy drilling and low to moderate capacity micropiles, a typical crew may install up to 6 to 20 micropiles of 15 m (50 ft) length (maximum) per day, and labor may be 25 to 30 percent of the total project cost. In tight access areas and difficult drilling conditions labor may rise to 30 to 45 percent of the total cost, and in extra labor-intensive projects where prevailing labor costs are high (e.g., major urban areas) up to 60 percent of the micropile costs.
key_points: Typical crew of four: project superintendent, drill operator and two laborers
Easy drilling, low to moderate capacity: 6 to 20 micropiles up to 15 m (50 ft) long per day; labor 25 to 30 percent of cost
Tight access and difficult drilling: labor 30 to 45 percent
Labor-intensive work with high prevailing labor costs (major urban areas): up to 60 percent
sections.applicability: Crew size, installation rates and labor share of micropile cost.

sections.title: Load Testing Costs
sections.summary: Load testing cost depends on access, type of test, number of tests, protocol (quick or standard) and required capacity. Compression tests always cost more than comparable tension tests because reaction piles or anchors are needed. Verification tests cost $10,000 (tension) to $25,000 (compression) per test; proof tests $6,000 to $10,000. With very difficult access and high capacities (more than 200 tons) a test could exceed $50,000.
sections.body: (p. 10-4) Load testing costs depend on site access, the type of testing (compression, tension and/or lateral), the number of tests, the testing protocol ('quick' or standard load tests) and the required load capacity. The engineer typically selects the number and type of tests, but compression tests will always cost more than a comparable (similar maximum load) tension test, mainly because reaction piles or anchors must be constructed. Verification load tests range from $10,000 to $25,000 per test, the lower end representative of tension tests and the upper end of compression tests. Proof tests, commonly carried to significantly lower loads and performed in less time, range from $6,000 to $10,000; these costs are representative of typical projects. Where very difficult access limits equipment, costs can be significantly higher: a high-capacity test in an easy access area may be about $25,000, whereas in difficult access areas with relatively high capacities to verify (e.g., greater than 200 tons) a test could exceed $50,000.
key_points: Load test cost depends on access, test type, number of tests, protocol (quick or standard) and required capacity
Compression tests always cost more than comparable tension tests because reaction piles or anchors are needed
Verification tests $10,000 (tension) to $25,000 (compression) per test
Proof tests $6,000 to $10,000 per test
Difficult access with capacities above 200 tons: tests could exceed $50,000
sections.applicability: Factors in and typical costs of micropile verification and proof load tests.

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: An Owner can apply the modifications in Table 10-4, developed from micropile contractor input, to the $300 per linear meter average for a preliminary estimate. Factors and influences: access 0 to +100 percent; geology 0 to +50; pile capacity -30 to +30; pile length -25 to +25; pile quantity -50 to +100; testing -10 to +10; mobilization 0 to +10; non-continuous drilling 0 to +25; union agreements -15 to +30; overhead and profit -10 to +100.
sections.body: (p. 10-5) An Owner considering micropiles may use the average cost of $300 per linear meter with the modifications in Table 10-4 to develop a preliminary cost estimate. Table 10-4 was developed from micropile contractor input and reflects the relative effect of project-specific factors on construction cost; its use is shown with two example projects (10.3.3), and the factors are discussed further in 10.3.2. Table 10-4 reference values: moderate pile capacity 1,000 kN (225 kips); average pile length 15 m (50 ft); average pile quantity 50; average testing one verification test and proof testing of 5 percent of all piles; a non-continuous drilling operation implies significant down time during drilling.

sections.title: Effects of Project-Specific Constraints on Cost
sections.summary: Access and ground conditions have a large effect, though they would affect driven piles and drilled shafts similarly. Higher capacity needs longer bond zones (possibly longer rock sockets) and more steel. Longer piles need more casing sections, possibly more robust equipment and more hole stabilization. Pile quantity gives the largest relative reduction (contractor backlog and staffing). Overhead and profit reflect perceived risk, likely high where other factors raise cost, especially difficult drilling and low productivity.
sections.body: (p. 10-6) The first two factors in Table 10-4, access and ground conditions, have a large effect on micropile cost, although difficult access and ground (e.g., drilling in excessively hard ground) would likely have similar implications for driven piles and drilled shafts. Pile capacity affects cost because higher capacity micropiles need longer bond zones, possibly longer rock sockets, and greater structural requirements (more steel area). Pile length affects cost because longer piles need more individual casing sections, beyond certain lengths more robust drilling equipment, and possibly more hole stabilization at depth. The most significant relative cost reduction in Table 10-4 is associated with pile quantities: large projects let the contractor define backlog and long-term personnel needs. The last entry, overhead and profit, relates to perceived contractor risk; it may be hard for an Owner to assess, but where other factors generally raise cost above average, it is reasonable to assume the contractor sees significant risk, especially where ground conditions are expected to give difficult drilling and low productivity.
key_points: Access and ground conditions have a large effect (similar for driven piles and drilled shafts)
Higher capacity needs longer bond zones (possibly longer rock sockets) and more steel
Longer piles: more casing sections, more robust equipment, more hole stabilization at depth
Pile quantity gives the largest relative cost reduction (contractor backlog and staffing)
Overhead and profit reflect perceived risk, likely high where other factors raise cost (difficult drilling, low productivity)
sections.applicability: Why access, ground, capacity, length, quantity and perceived risk change micropile cost.

sections.title: Sample Problem No. 1 (Bridge Abutment Support)
sections.summary: Single-span bridge in mountainous terrain about 125 km northwest of Denver: 12 CASE 1, Type B micropiles per abutment, ultimate 1,190 kN compression and 490 kN tension, about 12 m long; one compression verification test on a sacrificial pile and two proof tests; work benches to build; very difficult bond zone drilling in cobbles and boulders. Table 10-5 totals +85 percent: $300 x (1 + 85/100) = $555 per meter, or $6,660 per 12-m micropile.
sections.body: (pp. 10-6 to 10-7) Given: a single-span bridge in mountainous terrain about 125 km northwest of Denver, Colorado, each abutment supported on 12 CASE 1, Type B micropiles with ultimate capacities of 1,190 kN (270 kips) in compression and 490 kN (110 kips) in tension, about 12 m (40 ft) long. Testing: one verification load test (compression only) on a sacrificial pile and two proof tests. Access to each work bench must be established; drilling of the bond zone is expected to be very difficult because of cobbles and boulders; drilling is continuous at each location with an additional set-up at Abutment 2. Solution: evaluate each influence factor (Table 10-5) and apply it to the per-meter price: average cost = $300 x (1 + 85/100) = $555 per linear meter of micropile; for 12-m (40-ft) micropiles the unit price is $555 x 12 m = $6,660 each.

sections.title: Sample Problem No. 2 (Seismic Retrofit)
sections.summary: Seismic retrofit of a 200-m concrete viaduct in San Francisco: 30 footings with 12 Type B micropiles each (360), ultimate 2,500 kN compression and 1,500 kN tension, about 20 m long through 10 to 12 m of medium dense silty sands into weathered serpentine; one compression verification test and 30 proof tests; good access, 5 to 12 m headroom, continuous drilling. Table 10-6 totals +10 percent: $300 x (1 + 10/100) = $330 per meter, or $6,600 per 20-m micropile.
sections.body: (p. 10-8) Given: seismic retrofit of a 200-m (650-ft) long concrete viaduct in San Francisco, California; 30 footings with 12 Type B micropiles per footing (360 micropiles), ultimate capacities 2,500 kN (560 kips) in compression and 1,500 kN (340 kips) in tension. The subsurface has about 10 to 12 m (printed '(330 to 40 ft)') of medium dense silty sands over weathered to moderately weathered serpentine bedrock; micropiles average about 20 m (66 ft) long. Testing: one verification test (compression only) on a sacrificial pile and 30 proof tests. Access to each pile location is good, overhead clearance varies from 5 to 12 m (16 to 40 ft) per footing, and drilling is assumed continuous with setups between footings. Solution: evaluate each influence factor (Table 10-6): average cost = $300 x (1 + 10/100) = $330 per linear meter of micropile; for 20-m micropiles the unit price is $330 x 20 = $6,600 each.

sections.title: Measurement and Payment for Micropiles
sections.summary: Table 10-7 lists typical pay items: mobilization/demobilization and preproduction test pile program lump sum; verification and proof tests per each; foundation support micropiles per each; slope stabilization micropiles per lineal meter of cap beam. Design-build may use lump sums. Alternatives: pay per unit length, or per pile with add/deduct for length. In karst, pay for grout above a minimum, with no extra pay up to twice the theoretical volume; obstructions may be paid by time and material.
sections.body: (pp. 10-8 to 10-10) Table 10-7 summarizes typical pay items for a micropile project; design-build projects may use lump sum units for most items. For the micropile itself, alternative pricing may be per unit length of micropile, or per pile with an add or deduct where actual lengths differ from a predetermined bid length. Additional pay items will be required where difficult ground may cause problems anticipated at bid. For example, in karstic regions a pay item should be developed for grout volume above some minimum, but specifications should require no additional compensation where grout volumes are no greater than two times the theoretical drillhole volume, i.e., the per-pile cost includes grout up to twice the theoretical volume. If obstructions are anticipated, the specifications should include a pay item for their removal, which may be on a time and material basis; then it is important to use a contractor experienced in similar ground and to provide full-time inspection during removal, and whenever time and material payment may be used, the Owner should request detailed labor and material charges with the contractor's bid.
key_points: Table 10-7: mobilization/demobilization and preproduction test pile program, lump sum
Table 10-7: verification and proof load tests, per each; foundation support micropiles, per each
